interest: This file is exceptionally valuable for historians of modern Japan and colonial Korea because it illuminates the legal contradictions and bureaucratic mechanisms of intra-imperial migration during the Great Depression. While Japan's official ideology posited Koreans as imperial subjects entitled to freedom of movement, the reality of intense domestic labor competition, social prejudice, and security fears led authorities to covertly restrict migration through police-administered sailing certificates (toko shomeisho) rather than overt legislation. A fascinating revelation is the State Department Visa Division's internal memorandum observing that Japan had 'taken a leaf from our book' by adapting the American administrative 'public charge' doctrine to exclude colonial subjects without enacting discriminatory laws. Furthermore, the file provides rich contemporary statistical data on land tenancy in Chosen and details colonial initiatives to divert destitute rural laborers toward Manchuria and northern Korea.
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.5595) covers the period from May 1930 to December 1934 and documents the socio-economic, political, and administrative problems surrounding Korean immigration into Japan proper. Consisting of diplomatic despatches, embassy and consular reports, press translations, and internal State Department memoranda from Tokyo, Seoul, and Washington, the file tracks the rapid expansion of the Korean population in Japan from 40,000 in 1920 to over 450,000 (with unofficial estimates reaching 700,000) by 1934. The documents detail the severe agrarian crisis and land tenancy system in Korea that compelled hundreds of thousands of destitute peasants to seek employment in Japan, the intense friction and wage competition with domestic Japanese labor during the Great Depression, the legacy of anti-Korean violence following the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake, and the Japanese government's reliance on police-administered sailing certificates ('toko shomeisho') under a public charge standard to restrict the entry of imperial subjects without passing discriminatory legislation.

subfiles.about: Transmittal despatch forwarding an American Embassy report on Korean immigration into Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador William R. Castle, Jr. submits to the Secretary of State a staff report entitled 'Korean Immigration into Japan.' The transmittal despatch carries departmental routing stamps showing distribution and review by the Visa Office and the Office of the Economic Adviser in June 1930.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 139 from Tokyo Transmitting Report on Korean Immigration

subfiles.about: Comprehensive embassy report examining the historical, demographic, economic, and social dimensions of Korean migration into Japan.
subfiles.summary: This embassy report details Korean migration from early historical interactions through the post-annexation surge spurred by World War I industrial growth and post-1923 Tokyo earthquake reconstruction. It documents that roughly 250,000 Koreans were living in Japan by 1930, predominantly concentrated in major industrial urban centers such as Osaka, Fukuoka, and Tokyo. The report highlights severe racial discrimination, wage differentials of approximately twenty percent below Japanese peers, and the violent aftermath of the 1923 earthquake when hundreds of Koreans were massacred. It also discusses the legal predicament confronting Japanese authorities, who hesitated to formally ban the movement of imperial subjects despite vocal opposition from domestic labor unions during the depression.
subfiles.title: Embassy Report: Korean Immigration into Japan

subfiles.about: Consular despatch analyzing Korean emigration to Japan, police sailing certificates, and rural land tenancy in Korea.
subfiles.summary: Consul William R. Langdon reports on the estimated 400,000 to 700,000 Koreans residing in Japan, emphasizing the growing social and economic tensions resulting from their employment as cheap labor. He explains that because imperial law prevents legislative prohibition of internal migration, the authorities instituted administrative restrictions requiring prospective migrants to secure a police sailing certificate ('toko shomeisho') by proving financial self-sufficiency or prearranged employment. Langdon provides detailed agrarian statistics showing that over 80 percent of Korean farmers own no land and more than two-thirds of paddy fields are worked by tenants, concluding that chronic rural impoverishment drives mass migration to Japan and Manchuria.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 22 from Seoul: Korean Emigration to Japan

subfiles.about: Summarized translations of Seoul newspaper articles discussing administrative restrictions on emigration to Japan and surplus labor relocation.
subfiles.summary: These four press translations from the Dong-A Ilbo and Chosen Ilbo report on intensifying official restrictions on Korean laborers traveling to Japan. They describe joint police conferences held in Tokyo between Home Ministry and Chosen officials to coordinate the strict issuance of toko shomeisho, plan the relief or repatriation of unemployed Koreans, treat opium addicts, and suppress communist organizers. The articles also discuss government plans to divert surplus labor from southern Korea to industrial and hydroelectric projects in the northern provinces, while expressing editorial indignation at discriminatory barriers placed on fellow imperial subjects.
subfiles.title: Press Translations Enclosed with Despatch No. 22 on Emigration Restrictions

subfiles.about: Official summary sheet summarizing the contents and conclusions of Seoul Despatch No. 22.
subfiles.summary: A duplicate two-page consulate summary sheet providing an abstract of Consul Langdon's Despatch No. 22 of June 8, 1934. It summarizes the estimate of 400,000 to 700,000 Koreans in Japan, the administrative control through toko shomeisho sailing certificates, and the desperate landlessness of 80 percent of Korean peasants driving emigration. The summary also notes the demographic irony that Korea has gained more population relief from annexation than Japan.
subfiles.title: Summary of Seoul Despatch No. 22 on Korean Emigration to Japan

subfiles.about: Certified duplicate copy of Consul Langdon's Despatch No. 22 accompanied by duplicate copies of its first two press enclosures.
subfiles.summary: A verified record copy ('In quintuplicate') of Despatch No. 22 from Consul William R. Langdon at Seoul, together with duplicate copies of Enclosures Nos. 1 and 2 from the Dong-A Ilbo. The document reproduces Langdon's analysis of Korean migration, agrarian land tenure data, the administrative mechanism of police sailing certificates, and plans to shift surplus labor to northern Chosen.
subfiles.title: Duplicate Copy of Seoul Despatch No. 22 with Enclosures Nos. 1 and 2

subfiles.about: Stray non-record sheet bearing multiple receipt stamps from the Veterans Administration and Council of the Air Force.
subfiles.from: Veterans Administration / Council of the Air Force
subfiles.summary: A miscellaneous backing sheet containing multiple stamped date marks from May 22, 1934, indicating receipt by the Veterans Administration Mail Subdivision ('Reader 11') and the 'Counsel of the Council for the Department of the Air Force.' The page is extraneous to diplomatic reporting on Japanese internal affairs and was erroneously interfiled or filmed during microfilming.
subfiles.title: Veterans Administration / Council of the Air Force Receipt Sheet

subfiles.about: Internal State Department memorandum comparing Japanese administrative restrictions on Korean migration to U.S. immigration practices.
subfiles.summary: A Visa Division memorandum to Mr. Simmons analyzing Consul Langdon's Despatch No. 22 on Korean emigration. The author, C.P.S., remarks that Japan appears to have 'taken a leaf from our book' by using an administrative principle—requiring migrants to satisfy police that they will not become a public charge in order to receive a sailing certificate—to bypass the legal impossibility of legislating against internal movement of subjects. The memorandum notes the particular interest of the Visa Division in these regulations and confirms that the report was rated 'GOOD' during departmental review.
subfiles.title: Visa Division Memorandum on Administrative Restrictions on Korean Migration

subfiles.about: State Department Document File Note cross-referencing Tokyo Report No. 143 filed under decimal classification 894.55/4.
subfiles.summary: A State Department Document File Note recording that Report No. 143 from Tokyo, dated October 19, 1934, by Vice Consul John M. Allison, is filed under decimal classification 894.55/4. The note states that the report replies to the Department's Circular Instruction of June 1, 1934, regarding the 'Trend of Migratory Movement, from Korea into Japan,' and cross-references the attached excerpt filed under 894.5595.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Tokyo Report No. 143 on Korean Migratory Movements

subfiles.about: Excerpt from Tokyo Report No. 143 detailing historical migration statistics and Japanese police regulations on Korean labor.
subfiles.summary: This two-page extract (pages 24-25 of Report No. 143) reviews Japanese legal control over Korean laborers from the 1899 alien labor ordinance through the post-1910 annexation era. It explains that travel certificate restrictions were lifted in 1922 but reimposed by police regulations in October 1925 because technical rights of imperial subjects precluded formal statutory exclusion. Citing police statistics from Fusan, the extract demonstrates that between 1917 and 1927 there was a net increase of 194,832 Koreans in Japan, creating an annual net immigration that exceeded Japan's total net emigration abroad even when including migration to Hokkaido and Sakhalin.
subfiles.title: Excerpt from Tokyo Report No. 143: Korean Migration Statistics and Regulations

subfiles.about: Consular report transmitting and analyzing newly obtained Japanese Home Ministry figures on Korean immigration from 1929 to 1933.
subfiles.summary: Vice Consul John M. Allison, approved by Consul General Arthur Garrels, submits Voluntary Report No. 148 supplementing Report No. 143 on migratory movements. Allison reports that an official in the American Section of the Japanese Foreign Ministry provided a Ministry of Home Affairs study covering Korean migration from 1929 through 1933. He observes that the annual net increase of Koreans in Japan accelerated to over 44,000, almost double Japan's average annual emigration abroad, and notes the emerging entry of Koreans into skilled trades as well as Japanese anxieties over appearing discriminatory toward colonial subjects.
subfiles.title: Report No. 148: Korean Immigration into Japan Proper

subfiles.about: Translation of an official Japanese Home Ministry study on Korean population figures, labor market impact, and administrative relief.
subfiles.summary: This translated Home Ministry report places the Korean population in Japan proper at 456,000 officially (and approximately 600,000 realistically) at the end of 1933, noting annual increases as high as 79,000 in 1932. It describes how the influx of Korean laborers during the depression depressed domestic wages and caused distress among Japanese workers, particularly as Koreans increasingly entered skilled labor. While affirming that Japan adheres to non-discrimination within the empire, the report explains that the Chosen Government-General actively dissuades destitute Koreans who cannot speak Japanese and lack employment prospects from leaving Korea, an administrative intervention often misinterpreted as unlawful exclusion.
subfiles.title: Translation of Japanese Home Ministry Report on Korean Immigrants in Japan Proper
